title: Relative Formula Mass and Moles
description: Calculate Mr from formulae, convert between mass and moles, and find percentage composition by mass.

method_card.title: Relative Formula Mass and Moles
method_card.content:
These calculations underpin every chemistry calculation you will meet at GCSE. If you can't do these quickly and accurately, multi-step problems become very difficult.

Approach:

  • To find \(M_r\), add up every atom's \(A_r\) — don't forget subscripts and brackets
  • Brackets multiply everything inside: Ca(OH)₂ means 2 × O and 2 × H
  • Moles links mass to formula mass — rearrange the triangle depending on what you need
  • Percentage composition asks what fraction of the total mass comes from one element

Common pitfalls:

  • Forgetting to multiply inside brackets — Ca(OH)₂ has 2 oxygen atoms, not 1
  • Using the wrong \(A_r\) value — double-check the periodic table
  • Confusing moles and mass — moles is a count, mass is in grams
  • For percentage composition, divide by the total \(M_r\), not just part of it
steps: Write out the formula and identify every atom present
Look up each Ar value and multiply by the number of atoms (watch brackets!)
Add them all up to get Mr
To find moles: divide mass by Mr. To find mass: multiply moles by Mr
State your answer with the correct unit (no unit for Mr, mol for moles, g for mass, % for composition)

exam_context.frequency: Every exam — Mr and moles appear on every Paper 1

worked_examples.question: Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of magnesium oxide, MgO. (Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16)

steps.label: Step 1 — Identify the atoms
steps.content: MgO contains 1 magnesium atom and 1 oxygen atom.

worked_examples.question: Calculate the number of moles in 14.8 g of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂. (Ar: Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1)
Calculate the percentage by mass of iron in iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃. (Ar: Fe = 56, O = 16)

steps.label: Step 2 — Find the mass contribution of iron

bronze.display: Calculate the relative formula mass (\(M_r\)) of sodium chloride, NaCl. (\(A_r\): Na = 23, Cl = 35.5)

misconceptions.message: Check your Ar values. Na = 23 and Cl = 35.5, so Mr = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5.

bronze.display: Calculate the relative formula mass (\(M_r\)) of water, H₂O. (\(A_r\): H = 1, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: There are 2 hydrogen atoms in H₂O. Mr = 2 × 1 + 16 = 18.

bronze.display: Calculate the relative formula mass (\(M_r\)) of carbon dioxide, CO₂. (\(A_r\): C = 12, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: CO₂ has 2 oxygen atoms. Mr = 12 + 2 × 16 = 12 + 32 = 44.

bronze.display: Calculate the relative formula mass (\(M_r\)) of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃. (\(A_r\): Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: CaCO₃ has 3 oxygen atoms. Mr = 40 + 12 + 3 × 16 = 40 + 12 + 48 = 100.

bronze.display: Calculate the number of moles in 36 g of water, H₂O. (\(M_r\) of H₂O = 18)

misconceptions.message: Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 36 ÷ 18 = 2 mol. Don't multiply — divide.

bronze.display: Calculate the number of moles in 5.5 g of carbon dioxide, CO₂. (\(M_r\) of CO₂ = 44)

misconceptions.message: Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 5.5 ÷ 44 = 0.125 mol.

bronze.display: Calculate the number of moles in 4.8 g of magnesium oxide, MgO. (\(M_r\) of MgO = 40)

misconceptions.message: Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 4.8 ÷ 40 = 0.12 mol.

bronze.display: Calculate the mass of 0.5 mol of water, H₂O. (\(M_r\) of H₂O = 18)

misconceptions.message: Mass = moles × Mr = 0.5 × 18 = 9 g. Multiply, don't divide.

silver.display: Calculate the relative formula mass (\(M_r\)) of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂. (\(A_r\): Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: The bracket means 2 × (O + H) = 2 × (16 + 1) = 34. Mr = 40 + 34 = 74.
Ca(OH)₂ has TWO OH groups. Mr = 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 74, not 57.

silver.display: Calculate the relative formula mass (\(M_r\)) of magnesium nitrate, Mg(NO₃)₂. (\(A_r\): Mg = 24, N = 14, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: The bracket multiplies everything inside by 2: 2 × (14 + 3 × 16) = 2 × 62 = 124. Mr = 24 + 124 = 148.

silver.display: Calculate the number of moles in 11.7 g of sodium chloride, NaCl. (\(M_r\) of NaCl = 58.5)

misconceptions.message: Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 11.7 ÷ 58.5 = 0.2 mol.

silver.display: Calculate the number of moles in 25 g of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃. (\(M_r\) of CaCO₃ = 100)

misconceptions.message: Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25 mol.

silver.display: Calculate the mass of 0.25 mol of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃. (\(M_r\) of CaCO₃ = 100)

misconceptions.message: Mass = moles × Mr = 0.25 × 100 = 25 g. Multiply, don't divide.

silver.display: Calculate the mass of 0.4 mol of sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃. (\(A_r\): Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16)

gold.display: Calculate the percentage by mass of calcium in calcium carbonate, CaCO₃. (\(A_r\): Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: Remember to multiply by 100 to convert the fraction to a percentage.

gold.display: Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in potassium nitrate, KNO₃. Give your answer to 1 d.p. (\(A_r\): K = 39, N = 14, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: Make sure you're finding the percentage of nitrogen (Ar = 14), not potassium or oxygen.

gold.display: Calculate the percentage by mass of oxygen in water, H₂O. Give your answer to 1 d.p. (\(A_r\): H = 1, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: The question asks for oxygen, not hydrogen. % O = (16 ÷ 18) × 100 = 88.9%.

gold.display: A sample of a compound contains 0.1 mol and has a mass of 7.1 g. Calculate the relative formula mass of the compound.

misconceptions.message: Mr = mass ÷ moles = 7.1 ÷ 0.1 = 71. Rearrange moles = mass ÷ Mr to find Mr.
Rearrange: if moles = mass ÷ Mr, then Mr = mass ÷ moles = 7.1 ÷ 0.1 = 71.

gold.display: A scientist has 0.05 mol of a compound with a mass of 4.9 g. Calculate the \(M_r\) of the compound and suggest its identity. (\(M_r\): H₂SO₄ = 98, HNO₃ = 63, HCl = 36.5, NaOH = 40)

misconceptions.message: Mr = mass ÷ moles = 4.9 ÷ 0.05 = 98. This matches H₂SO₄.
Rearrange: Mr = mass ÷ moles = 4.9 ÷ 0.05 = 98.

gold.display: Calculate the mass of 3 mol of carbon dioxide, CO₂. (\(A_r\): C = 12, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: Mass = moles × Mr = 3 × 44 = 132 g. Multiply, don't divide.

title: Balancing Equations and Reacting Masses
description: Balance chemical equations, use mole ratios from balanced equations to calculate reacting masses and products formed.

method_card.title: Balancing Equations and Reacting Masses
method_card.content:
Reacting mass questions follow a fixed four-step method every time. Master the method and you can tackle any question — the chemistry changes, but the maths never does.

Approach:

  • Always start from a balanced equation — the big numbers in front of formulae tell you the mole ratio
  • The mole ratio is the bridge between two substances — it tells you how many moles of product you get from a given number of moles of reactant
  • If the question gives you a mass, convert to moles first. If it asks for a mass, convert from moles at the end.

Common pitfalls:

  • Using an unbalanced equation — the ratio will be wrong and your answer will be wrong
  • Confusing the coefficients (big numbers) with subscripts (small numbers)
  • Forgetting to convert between moles and mass at the start and end
  • Using the \(M_r\) of the wrong substance when converting back to mass
  • In limiting reactant problems, always check both reactants — the one that runs out first limits the product
steps: Write or check the balanced equation — get the mole ratio
Calculate the moles of the substance you know (moles = mass ÷ Mr)
Use the mole ratio to find the moles of the substance you want
Convert back to mass if needed (mass = moles × Mr)
State your answer with the correct unit

exam_context.frequency: Almost every exam — a common 4–5 mark multi-step question

worked_examples.question: Balance this equation: Mg + O₂ → MgO

steps.label: Step 1 — Count atoms on each side
steps.content: Left: 1 Mg, 2 O. Right: 1 Mg, 1 O. Oxygen is unbalanced.

steps.label: Step 2 — Balance oxygen
steps.content: Put a 2 in front of MgO → Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Now right has 2 Mg, so balance Mg too.

worked_examples.question: Calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Calculate the mass of calcium oxide (CaO) produced from 25 g of CaCO₃. (Ar: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
12 g of magnesium reacts with 12 g of oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Which reactant is the limiting reactant? Calculate the mass of MgO formed. (Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16)

steps.label: Step 1 — Find moles of each reactant
steps.content: Moles of Mg = 12 ÷ 24 = 0.5 mol. Moles of O₂ = 12 ÷ 32 = 0.375 mol.

steps.label: Step 2 — Use the ratio to check which runs out
steps.content:
Ratio is 2 Mg : 1 O₂. So 0.5 mol Mg needs 0.25 mol O₂. We have 0.375 mol O₂ — plenty.

0.375 mol O₂ would need 0.75 mol Mg. We only have 0.5 mol Mg — Mg is limiting.

steps.label: Step 3 — Calculate product from limiting reactant
steps.content: 0.5 mol Mg → 0.5 mol MgO (2:2 ratio). Mass = 0.5 × 40

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Mg is the limiting reactant. Mass of MgO = 20 g

bronze.display: Balance this equation: Na + Cl₂ → NaCl. What number goes in front of Na?

misconceptions.message: Cl₂ has 2 chlorine atoms but NaCl has only 1. You need 2NaCl, which means you also need 2Na. Answer: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.

bronze.display: Balance this equation: Fe + O₂ → Fe₂O₃. What number goes in front of Fe?

misconceptions.message: Balanced equation: 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃. Check: 4 Fe each side, 6 O each side.

bronze.display: Balance this equation: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O. What number goes in front of H₂?

misconceptions.message: Balanced: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Check: 4 H each side, 2 O each side.

bronze.display: In the equation 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, what is the mole ratio of Mg to MgO?

misconceptions.message: The coefficients are 2Mg and 2MgO. The ratio is 2:2, which simplifies to 1:1. Both '1:1' and '2:2' are correct.

bronze.display: In the equation N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, how many moles of NH₃ are produced from 1 mol of N₂?

misconceptions.message: The ratio of N₂ to NH₃ is 1:2. So 1 mol N₂ produces 2 mol NH₃.

bronze.display: In the equation CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, how many moles of CO₂ are produced from 3 mol of CaCO₃?

misconceptions.message: The ratio is 1:1. So 3 mol CaCO₃ produces 3 mol CO₂.

bronze.display: 4.8 g of magnesium reacts with oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Calculate the mass of MgO produced. (\(A_r\): Mg = 24, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: Moles of Mg = 4.8 ÷ 24 = 0.2. Ratio 2:2 (1:1), so 0.2 mol MgO. Mr of MgO = 40. Mass = 0.2 × 40 = 8 g.
Use Mr of MgO (= 40) to convert moles of MgO to mass, not Mr of Mg.

bronze.display: Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. Calculate the mass of hydrogen gas produced from 2.4 g of magnesium. (\(A_r\): Mg = 24, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: Moles Mg = 2.4 ÷ 24 = 0.1. Ratio 1:1. Mr of H₂ = 2. Mass = 0.1 × 2 = 0.2 g.
Use Mr of H₂ (= 2) to convert moles of H₂ to mass.

silver.display: Calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Calculate the mass of CO₂ produced from 25 g of CaCO₃. (\(A_r\): Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: Mr of CaCO₃ = 100, Mr of CO₂ = 44. Moles = 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25. Ratio 1:1. Mass = 0.25 × 44 = 11 g.
Convert to moles using Mr of CaCO₃ (100), then convert back using Mr of CO₂ (44).

silver.display: Sodium reacts with water: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. Calculate the mass of NaOH produced from 4.6 g of sodium. (\(A_r\): Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: Moles of Na = 4.6 ÷ 23 = 0.2. Ratio Na:NaOH = 2:2 = 1:1. Mr of NaOH = 40. Mass = 0.2 × 40 = 8 g.

silver.display: Iron(III) oxide is reduced: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Calculate the mass of iron produced from 32 g of Fe₂O₃. (\(A_r\): Fe = 56, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: Moles Fe₂O₃ = 32 ÷ 160 = 0.2. Ratio 1:2. Moles Fe = 0.4. Mass = 0.4 × 56 = 22.4 g.
Mr of Fe₂O₃ = 2 × 56 + 3 × 16 = 160. Mr of Fe = 56 (it's just the element).

silver.display: Aluminium reacts with copper sulfate: 2Al + 3CuSO₄ → Al₂(SO₄)₃ + 3Cu. Calculate the mass of copper produced from 5.4 g of aluminium. (\(A_r\): Al = 27, Cu = 64)

misconceptions.message: Moles of Al = 5.4 ÷ 27 = 0.2. Ratio Al:Cu = 2:3. Moles Cu = 0.2 × 3 ÷ 2 = 0.3. Mass = 0.3 × 64 = 19.2 g.
The ratio is 2 Al : 3 Cu. So multiply moles of Al by 3/2 to get moles of Cu.

silver.display: Nitrogen reacts with hydrogen: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Calculate the mass of ammonia (NH₃) produced from 5.6 g of nitrogen. (\(A_r\): N = 14, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: Mr of N₂ = 28, Mr of NH₃ = 17. Moles N₂ = 5.6 ÷ 28 = 0.2. Ratio 1:2. Moles NH₃ = 0.4. Mass = 0.4 × 17 = 6.8 g.

silver.display: Copper oxide reacts with sulfuric acid: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O. Calculate the mass of copper sulfate (CuSO₄) produced from 16 g of CuO. (\(A_r\): Cu = 64, O = 16, S = 32, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: Mr of CuO = 80, Mr of CuSO₄ = 160. Moles CuO = 16 ÷ 80 = 0.2. Ratio 1:1. Mass CuSO₄ = 0.2 × 160 = 32 g.

gold.display: 6.5 g of zinc reacts with excess hydrochloric acid: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. The mass of ZnCl₂ produced is 13.6 g. Calculate the mass of hydrogen gas produced using conservation of mass. (The total mass of HCl used is 7.3 g.)

misconceptions.message: Conservation of mass: total reactants = total products. (6.5 + 7.3) = (13.6 + H₂). H₂ = 13.8 − 13.6 = 0.2 g.
You don't need Mr here — just use conservation of mass. Reactant mass in = product mass out.

gold.display: 12 g of magnesium reacts with 12 g of oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Which is the limiting reactant? Enter Mg or O₂.

misconceptions.message: Moles Mg = 12 ÷ 24 = 0.5. Moles O₂ = 12 ÷ 32 = 0.375. Ratio: 2 Mg needs 1 O₂, so 0.5 mol Mg needs 0.25 mol O₂. We have 0.375 mol O₂ — enough. Mg is limiting because all 0.5 mol is used up.

gold.display: 12 g of magnesium reacts with 12 g of oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Calculate the mass of MgO formed. (\(A_r\): Mg = 24, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: Use the limiting reactant (Mg). Moles Mg = 0.5. Ratio 2:2 → 0.5 mol MgO. Mass = 0.5 × 40 = 20 g.

gold.display: In the reaction 2Al + 3CuSO₄ → Al₂(SO₄)₃ + 3Cu, a student reacts 2.7 g of aluminium with excess copper sulfate solution. Calculate the mass of copper produced. (\(A_r\): Al = 27, Cu = 64)

misconceptions.message: The ratio is 2:3, not 1:1. Multiply moles of Al by 3/2 to get moles of Cu.

gold.display: Zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. 6.5 g of zinc is added to excess acid. Calculate the volume of hydrogen gas produced at room temperature and pressure, where 1 mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³. (\(A_r\): Zn = 65, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: Moles of Zn = 6.5 ÷ 65 = 0.1. Ratio 1:1. Moles H₂ = 0.1. Volume = 0.1 × 24 = 2.4 dm³.
Mr of Zn = 65 (not 64, that's copper). Moles = 6.5 ÷ 65 = 0.1.

gold.display: Calcium reacts with water: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂. Calculate the mass of calcium hydroxide produced from 4 g of calcium. (\(A_r\): Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: Ca(OH)₂ has Mr = 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 74, not 57. Don't forget to multiply the bracket.

title: Bond Energy Calculations
description: Use bond energies to calculate the overall energy change of a reaction and determine whether it is exothermic or endothermic.

method_card.title: Bond Energy Calculations
method_card.content:
Bond energy calculations tell you the overall energy change of a reaction. The method is always the same: add up the energy needed to break bonds, subtract the energy released when new bonds form.

Approach:

  • Draw out the structural formulae of all reactants and products — this lets you count every bond
  • Breaking bonds is endothermic (takes energy in). Making bonds is exothermic (gives energy out).
  • If the answer is negative, more energy is released than absorbed — the reaction is exothermic
  • If the answer is positive, more energy is absorbed than released — the reaction is endothermic

Common pitfalls:

  • Miscounting bonds — especially in combustion reactions (count ALL C–H bonds in the fuel, ALL O=O bonds, ALL C=O and O–H bonds in the products)
  • Subtracting the wrong way round — it's always broken minus made
  • Forgetting to multiply bond energies by the number of bonds (e.g. 4 × C–H in CH₄, not just 1)
  • Confusing the sign: negative = exothermic, positive = endothermic
steps: Draw out structural formulae and count every bond in reactants and products
Add up the total energy to break all bonds in the reactants
Add up the total energy released when all bonds in the products are made
Calculate: energy change = bonds broken − bonds made
State the sign and whether the reaction is exothermic (−) or endothermic (+)

exam_context.frequency: Common — often appears as a 4–5 mark structured question

worked_examples.question: Calculate the overall energy change for: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. Bond energies: H–H = 436 kJ/mol, Cl–Cl = 242 kJ/mol, H–Cl = 431 kJ/mol.
Calculate the overall energy change for the combustion of methane: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Bond energies: C–H = 413, O=O = 498, C=O = 803, O–H = 464 kJ/mol.

steps.label: Step 1 — Bonds broken
steps.content:
CH₄: 4 × C–H = 4 × 413 = 1652 kJ
2O₂: 2 × O=O = 2 × 498 = 996 kJ
Total broken = 2648 kJ

steps.label: Step 2 — Bonds made
steps.content:
CO₂: 2 × C=O = 2 × 803 = 1606 kJ
2H₂O: 4 × O–H = 4 × 464 = 1856 kJ
Total made = 3462 kJ

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: ΔH = −814 kJ/mol (exothermic — more energy released making bonds than absorbed breaking them)

worked_examples.question: Calculate the energy change for the combustion of ethene: C₂H₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 2H₂O. Bond energies: C=C = 614, C–H = 413, O=O = 498, C=O = 803, O–H = 464 kJ/mol.

steps.label: Step 1 — Bonds broken
steps.content:
C₂H₄: 1 × C=C = 614, 4 × C–H = 1652. Total = 2266 kJ
3O₂: 3 × O=O = 1494 kJ
Total broken = 3760 kJ

steps.label: Step 2 — Bonds made
steps.content:
2CO₂: 4 × C=O = 3212 kJ
2H₂O: 4 × O–H = 1856 kJ
Total made = 5068 kJ

bronze.display: Calculate the total energy needed to break all bonds in the reactants for: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. Bond energies: H–H = 436, Cl–Cl = 242 kJ/mol.
bronze.equation_hint: \(\text{total broken} = \text{sum of all bond energies in reactants}\)

misconceptions.message: Only add up bonds in the REACTANTS (left side). Broken = 436 + 242 = 678 kJ.

bronze.display: Calculate the total energy released when all bonds are made in the products for: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. Bond energies: H–Cl = 431 kJ/mol.
bronze.equation_hint: \(\text{total made} = \text{sum of all bond energies in products}\)

misconceptions.message: There are 2 HCl molecules, so 2 × H–Cl bonds. Total made = 2 × 431 = 862 kJ.

bronze.display: Calculate the overall energy change (ΔH) for: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. Bond energies: H–H = 436, Cl–Cl = 242, H–Cl = 431 kJ/mol.

misconceptions.message: ΔH = broken − made = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ/mol. Don't subtract the other way round.
The answer is negative (−184), meaning the reaction is exothermic.

bronze.display: Is the reaction H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl exothermic or endothermic? (ΔH = −184 kJ/mol)

misconceptions.message: A negative ΔH means exothermic — more energy is released making new bonds than is absorbed breaking old ones.

bronze.display: Calculate the overall energy change for: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Bond energies: H–H = 436, O=O = 498, O–H = 464 kJ/mol.

misconceptions.message: 2H₂O has 4 O–H bonds (2 in each water molecule). Total made = 4 × 464 = 1856 kJ.

bronze.display: Calculate the overall energy change for: H₂ + Br₂ → 2HBr. Bond energies: H–H = 436, Br–Br = 193, H–Br = 366 kJ/mol.
Calculate the overall energy change for: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Bond energies: N≡N = 945, H–H = 436, N–H = 391 kJ/mol.

misconceptions.message: Broken: 1 × N≡N + 3 × H–H = 945 + 1308 = 2253 kJ. Made: 6 × N–H = 2346 kJ (2 NH₃ molecules, 3 N–H bonds each). ΔH = 2253 − 2346 = −93 kJ/mol.
2NH₃ has 6 N–H bonds total (3 per molecule × 2 molecules).

bronze.display: In the reaction 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, how many O–H bonds are formed in total?
bronze.equation_hint: \(\text{count all bonds in all product molecules}\)

misconceptions.message: There are 2 water molecules, each with 2 O–H bonds. Total = 2 × 2 = 4 O–H bonds.
Don't confuse the number of molecules with the number of bonds. 2H₂O = 2 molecules × 2 bonds each = 4 bonds.

silver.display: Calculate the overall energy change for the combustion of methane: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Bond energies: C–H = 413, O=O = 498, C=O = 803, O–H = 464 kJ/mol.

misconceptions.message: 2H₂O has 4 O–H bonds, not 2. Each water molecule has 2 O–H bonds.

silver.display: The combustion of methane (CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O) has ΔH = −814 kJ/mol. The total energy to break all bonds in the reactants is 2648 kJ. Calculate the total energy released when bonds in the products are formed.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange: bonds made = bonds broken − ΔH = 2648 − (−814) = 2648 + 814 = 3462 kJ.

silver.display: A reaction has bonds broken = 1845 kJ and bonds made = 2130 kJ. Calculate ΔH and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.

misconceptions.message: ΔH = 1845 − 2130 = −285 kJ/mol. Negative = exothermic.
More energy is released making bonds (2130 kJ) than absorbed breaking them (1845 kJ), so it's exothermic (negative).

silver.display: A reaction has bonds broken = 1520 kJ and bonds made = 1380 kJ. Calculate ΔH and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.

misconceptions.message: ΔH = 1520 − 1380 = +140 kJ/mol. Positive = endothermic — more energy absorbed than released.

silver.display: Calculate the overall energy change for the combustion of hydrogen: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Bond energies: H–H = 436, O=O = 498, O–H = 464 kJ/mol. How many O–H bonds are formed in total?
silver.equation_hint: \(\text{count all bonds in all product molecules}\)

misconceptions.message: 2H₂O means two water molecules. Each has 2 O–H bonds, so 2 × 2 = 4 O–H bonds total.

silver.display: A student calculates ΔH for a reaction and gets +320 kJ/mol. Which statement is correct?
options: More energy is released making bonds than breaking bonds
More energy is absorbed breaking bonds than making bonds
The reaction gives out heat to the surroundings
The products are at a lower energy level than the reactants

misconceptions.message: Positive ΔH means more energy is absorbed breaking bonds than released making them. The reaction is endothermic — it takes in heat from the surroundings.

gold.display: Calculate the overall energy change for the combustion of ethene: C₂H₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 2H₂O. Bond energies: C=C = 614, C–H = 413, O=O = 498, C=O = 803, O–H = 464 kJ/mol.

misconceptions.message: C₂H₄ has 4 C–H bonds (2 on each carbon) and 1 C=C bond.

gold.display: Calculate the overall energy change for the combustion of ethane: 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O. Bond energies: C–C = 347, C–H = 413, O=O = 498, C=O = 803, O–H = 464 kJ/mol. Give the answer per mole of C₂H₆ (divide your total by 2).

misconceptions.message: The equation uses 2 mol of C₂H₆, so divide your total ΔH by 2 to get the answer per mole.

gold.display: The overall energy change for a reaction is −285 kJ/mol. The total energy to break bonds in the reactants is 1845 kJ. Calculate the total energy released when new bonds form in the products.

misconceptions.message: ΔH = broken − made. Rearrange: made = broken − ΔH = 1845 − (−285) = 1845 + 285 = 2130 kJ.
Be careful with the negative sign. Subtracting −285 means adding 285.

gold.display: A reaction has ΔH = +140 kJ/mol. The energy released forming product bonds is 1380 kJ. Calculate the total energy needed to break all reactant bonds.

misconceptions.message: ΔH = broken − made. Rearrange: broken = ΔH + made = 140 + 1380 = 1520 kJ.

gold.display: Reaction A has ΔH = −184 kJ/mol. Reaction B has ΔH = −814 kJ/mol. Which reaction releases more energy per mole? Enter A or B.

misconceptions.message: −814 is more negative than −184, so Reaction B releases more energy. A larger negative number means more exothermic.
Compare the size (magnitude) of the negative values: 814 > 184, so B releases more energy.

gold.display: Methane combustion (CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O) has ΔH = −814 kJ/mol. Hydrogen combustion (2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O) has ΔH = −486 kJ/mol. Which fuel releases more energy per gram? (\(M_r\): CH₄ = 16, H₂ = 2). Enter CH₄ or H₂.

misconceptions.message: Per gram of CH₄: 814 ÷ 16 = 50.9 kJ/g. Per gram of H₂: 486 ÷ (2 × 2) = 486 ÷ 4 = 121.5 kJ/g. H₂ releases more energy per gram, even though CH₄ releases more per mole.

title: Rates from Graphs and Concentrations
description: Calculate mean rates of reaction, read rates from graphs, and work out concentrations in g/dm³.

method_card.title: Rates from Graphs and Concentrations
method_card.content:
Rate of reaction questions test whether you can extract data from graphs and apply a simple formula. The maths is straightforward — the challenge is reading the graph accurately and converting units correctly.

Approach:

  • Mean rate is always change in quantity divided by time — whether the quantity is volume of gas, mass lost, or amount of product formed
  • For graphs, read values carefully from the axes — don't estimate if you can read exactly
  • The steeper the curve, the faster the reaction. A flat line means the reaction has finished.
  • Concentration is mass per unit volume — but watch whether the volume is in dm³ or cm³

Common pitfalls:

  • Not converting cm³ to dm³ for concentration (divide by 1000)
  • Reading the wrong axis on a graph
  • Confusing initial rate (steepest part at the start) with mean rate (total change ÷ total time)
  • Forgetting units — rate must have a unit of quantity per unit of time
steps: Identify what quantity is changing (volume, mass, concentration) and read the values
Find the change in quantity and the time period
Calculate: rate = change in quantity ÷ time
For concentration: check whether volume is in dm³ or cm³ (÷ 1000 to convert)
State your answer with the correct unit (e.g. cm³/s, g/s, g/dm³)

exam_context.frequency: Common — rate graphs appear frequently on Paper 2

worked_examples.question: A reaction produces 48 cm³ of gas in 60 seconds. Calculate the mean rate of reaction.
The graph below shows the volume of gas produced over time. Calculate the mean rate of reaction over the first 20 seconds.

steps.label: Step 1 — Read from the graph
steps.content: At t = 0 s, volume = 0 cm³. At t = 20 s, volume = 22 cm³.

worked_examples.question: 7.3 g of hydrochloric acid is dissolved in 250 cm³ of water. Calculate the concentration in g/dm³.

bronze.display: A reaction produces 48 cm³ of gas in 60 seconds. Calculate the mean rate of reaction.

misconceptions.message: Rate = quantity ÷ time = 48 ÷ 60 = 0.8 cm³/s. Don't divide time by quantity.

bronze.display: A reaction produces 35 cm³ of gas in 50 seconds. Calculate the mean rate of reaction.

misconceptions.message: Rate = 35 ÷ 50 = 0.7 cm³/s.

bronze.display: In a reaction, the mass of a flask decreases by 0.72 g over 120 seconds as gas escapes. Calculate the mean rate of mass loss.
10 g of salt is dissolved in 2 dm³ of water. Calculate the concentration.

misconceptions.message: Concentration = mass ÷ volume = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 g/dm³.

bronze.display: 4 g of sodium hydroxide is dissolved in 0.5 dm³ of water. Calculate the concentration.

misconceptions.message: Concentration = mass ÷ volume = 4 ÷ 0.5 = 8 g/dm³.

bronze.display: A reaction produces 56 cm³ of gas in 40 seconds. Calculate the mean rate of reaction.

misconceptions.message: Rate = 56 ÷ 40 = 1.4 cm³/s.

bronze.display: Use the graph. What is the total volume of gas produced by the end of the reaction?
bronze.equation_hint: \(\text{read the final volume from the graph}\)

misconceptions.message: The graph levels off at 42 cm³ (from 60 s onwards). This is the total volume produced.

bronze.display: 20 g of copper sulfate is dissolved in 0.4 dm³ of water. Calculate the concentration.

misconceptions.message: Concentration = mass ÷ volume = 20 ÷ 0.4 = 50 g/dm³.

silver.display: Use the graph. Calculate the mean rate of reaction over the first 20 seconds.

misconceptions.message: At 20 s, volume = 22 cm³. Rate = 22 ÷ 20 = 1.1 cm³/s.
Use only the first 20 seconds, not the total time. Rate = 22 ÷ 20 = 1.1 cm³/s.

silver.display: Use the graph. Calculate the mean rate of reaction between 10 s and 30 s.

misconceptions.message: At 10 s volume = 12 cm³, at 30 s volume = 30 cm³. Rate = (30 − 12) ÷ (30 − 10) = 18 ÷ 20 = 0.9 cm³/s.
Use the CHANGE in volume (30 − 12 = 18 cm³), not the value at 30 s.

silver.display: 7.3 g of hydrochloric acid is dissolved in 250 cm³ of water. Calculate the concentration in g/dm³.

misconceptions.message: Convert cm³ to dm³ first: 250 ÷ 1000 = 0.25 dm³. Then 7.3 ÷ 0.25 = 29.2 g/dm³.
250 cm³ is NOT the same as 250 dm³. Divide by 1000: 250 cm³ = 0.25 dm³.

silver.display: 5.85 g of sodium chloride is dissolved in 500 cm³ of water. Calculate the concentration in g/dm³.

misconceptions.message: Convert: 500 cm³ = 0.5 dm³. Concentration = 5.85 ÷ 0.5 = 11.7 g/dm³.
500 cm³ = 0.5 dm³. Don't forget to convert before dividing.

silver.display: Use the graph. Calculate the mean rate of mass loss over the first 40 seconds.

misconceptions.message: At 40 s, mass loss = 0.28 g. Rate = 0.28 ÷ 40 = 0.007 g/s.

silver.display: Use the graph. At what time does the reaction finish? (When the graph becomes flat.)
silver.equation_hint: \(\text{reaction finishes when the line goes flat}\)

misconceptions.message: The mass loss stops increasing between 100 s and 120 s (both read 0.48 g). The reaction finishes at about 100 s.

gold.display: The graph shows two reactions using the same chemicals. Calculate the mean rate of Reaction A over the first 10 seconds.

misconceptions.message: Read Reaction A (red line). At 10 s, volume = 24 cm³. Rate = 24 ÷ 10 = 2.4 cm³/s.
Use only the first 10 seconds, not the total time.

gold.display: Using the same graph, calculate the mean rate of Reaction B over the first 10 seconds.

misconceptions.message: Read Reaction B (blue line). At 10 s, volume = 15 cm³. Rate = 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5 cm³/s.

gold.display: Both reactions produce the same total volume (58 cm³). Suggest why Reaction A has a higher initial rate than Reaction B. Which factor could explain this?
options: Reaction A used a higher concentration of acid
Reaction A used a different acid
Reaction A was carried out at a lower temperature

misconceptions.message: Same total volume means same amount of reactant was used. A higher initial rate but same final volume is best explained by higher concentration (more frequent collisions at the start, but same total moles of reactant).

gold.display: A solution has a concentration of 40 g/dm³. A student needs 8 g of solute. Calculate the volume of solution they need in cm³.

misconceptions.message: Volume = mass ÷ concentration = 8 ÷ 40 = 0.2 dm³. Convert to cm³: 0.2 × 1000 = 200 cm³.
Rearrange concentration = mass ÷ volume to get volume = mass ÷ concentration.

gold.display: Use the graph. Calculate the overall mean rate for the entire reaction (from 0 s until the reaction finishes at 60 s).

misconceptions.message: The reaction finishes at 60 s (where the line goes flat at 42 cm³). Mean rate = 42 ÷ 60 = 0.7 cm³/s.
The reaction finishes at 60 s, not 70 s. The line is flat from 60 to 70 — no more gas is produced. Rate = 42 ÷ 60 = 0.7 cm³/s.

gold.display: A hydrochloric acid solution has a concentration of 36 g/dm³. A student uses 500 cm³ of this solution. Calculate the mass of HCl dissolved in this volume.

misconceptions.message: Convert 500 cm³ to dm³: 500 ÷ 1000 = 0.5 dm³. Mass = concentration × volume = 36 × 0.5 = 18 g.
Rearrange: mass = concentration × volume = 36 × 0.5 = 18 g.
